title: The Letter to the Galatians
subtitle: Pros Galatas, “To the Galatians”
description: Paul’s most urgent letter, written in astonishment to churches he had founded, which were being persuaded that Gentile believers must be circumcised and keep the law of Moses to belong to God’s people. He tells his own story, from persecutor to apostle, and of the day he opposed Peter to his face at Antioch; argues from Abraham, who believed God, and from the cross, where Christ became a curse on our behalf; and declares a family in which there is no Jew or Greek, slave or free, male and female, but all are one in Christ Jesus. Then freedom that serves, the works of the flesh and the fruit of the Spirit, and a closing word in Paul’s own large letters: “far be it from me to boast of anything except the cross.” The letter Luther called his own. In the Open Word Bible, a new translation from the Greek given freely to the public domain, with an introduction to the letter’s shape and meaning and a conclusion on where to read next.

qa.question: What is the Letter to the Galatians?
qa.answer: The ninth book of the New Testament, a short letter from the apostle Paul to the churches of Galatia, in what is now central Turkey. It answers teachers who were telling Gentile believers that they must be circumcised and keep the law of Moses to belong fully to God’s people. Paul insists that a person is justified through faith in Jesus Christ, not by works of the law, and that those who belong to Christ are free, led by the Spirit and called to serve one another in love.

qa.question: Who wrote Galatians, and when?
qa.answer: The apostle Paul, who names himself in the first verse and writes the closing lines in his own hand (6:11). Almost all scholars accept that he wrote it. Its date depends on which Galatia he meant. If the churches were in the south of the Roman province, founded on the journey of Acts 13–14, it may have been written around AD 48–49, making it perhaps his earliest letter. If they were in the old Celtic territory to the north, it was probably written in the mid-50s, not long before Romans.

qa.question: What was the problem in the Galatian churches?
qa.answer: After Paul left, other teachers arrived who taught that Gentile believers must be circumcised and keep the law of Moses, apparently to be counted among Abraham’s children, and who questioned whether Paul was a true apostle. Paul says they are turning the Galatians to “a different gospel”, though “there is no second gospel” (1:6–7). For him, adding circumcision as a condition of belonging meant that Christ was no longer enough: “if righteousness comes through the law, then Christ died for nothing at all” (2:21).

qa.question: What does “justified by faith” mean in Galatians?
qa.answer: To be justified is to be declared in the right by God. In Galatians Paul says that “no one is justified by works of the law; a person is justified only through faith in Jesus Christ” (2:16), and he points to Abraham, who “believed God, and it was counted to him as righteousness” (3:6). Christians differ on some details, such as whether “works of the law” means good works in general or especially the marks that set Jews apart, like circumcision and food laws, and whether “faith in Christ” may also mean Christ’s own faithfulness; but all agree that our standing with God is his gift in Christ.

qa.question: What is the fruit of the Spirit?
qa.answer: The list in Galatians 5:22–23 of what the Holy Spirit produces in believers: love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faithfulness, gentleness and self-control. Paul sets it against “the works of the flesh”, and speaks of one fruit, not many, as if these nine qualities were a single harvest. Of them he says, “No law stands against things like these.”

qa.question: Which translation of the Bible is this?
qa.answer: The Open Word Bible, a new translation made directly from the Greek and dedicated to the public domain, printed here at its Balanced level, which aims to be accurate and to read naturally aloud. The reasoning behind each of its sentences, with the Greek beside it, is published at openwordbible.org. The introduction and conclusion were written for this edition.
